STATE NEWS.
Items Gathered from State Exchanges and Other Sources.
Weatherford had it 109 in the shade Thursday.

Dallas county draws $30,113 from the State school fund this year.

G. W. Vaugn has been appointed inspector at Eagle Pass.

Local option elections are being ordered all over the State.

Marshall talks of funding her city debt in 7 per cent 10 year bonds.

Texas drummers have taken out 315 State licenses during the past month.

Senator Coke made a hot speech against prohibition at Waco last night.

The Western Union Telegraph company has opened a business office in Temple.

The American Legion of Honor has organized a lodge of 30 members at Eagle Pass.

Panola County Court Commissioners have expended $2500 in bridge building this summer.

General rains throughout the Texas cotton belt are reported, and there are more to follow.

Wyatt, the negro rapist who has been hiding near Houston for the past week, has been captured.

Terrell has voted to erect suitable buildings and present them to the county in case the county seat is removed to that place.

The new opera house at Weatherford is being elegantly furnished, five large stone buildings are in progress and the own is making healthy progress.

The Land Board have started the Grass Commissioners on a tour of inspection, to ascertain who are violating the land enclosure act of 1884.

The damage claims pending against the Houston and Texas Central railway foot up $1,053,849. In addition to this the company have 46 suits on hand involving titles to 700 sections of land.

A war of races is reported from Van Zandt county. The whites have raided the negro houses in Canton, considerable shooting has been indulged in, and a negro church burned in the southern part of the county. An obnoxious negro politician is said to be the cause of the trouble. Two negroes were killed.

There is trouble brewing between the Dallas city marshal and the Estelles of Fort Worth over the unfounded sensational report of a confession of murder by Jeff Estelle, who died at Grand Prairie last December. Marshal Arnold is accused of starting the report which was published in the Globe-Democrat, and that journal is threatened with a libel suit.
canton-canton-1885-08.A3:
Canton.
Ben Fullbright, one of the leading negroes of the county, was at old man Jim Ross', and it seemed that he (Fullbright) was the negro the crowd was after, but becoming frightened he left the premises. It is said Fullbright and others recognized several of the persons in the crowd. Ben Fullbright resides in the suburbs of Canton, and is said to be very offensive to a large class of white men. Some unknown person or persons visited his house last Wednesday night and shot him in the shoulder with twelve buckshot, sticking the muzzle of the gun through a crack of his house. But on entering the house one of the party shot Bob Prewitt in the back as he stepped into Fullbright's house. He fell, face forward, on the floor, and died on Saturday morning following. So far as THE HERALD correspondent has been informed, there are no charges against either of the negroes that justifies such rash acts. A coroner's jury of inquest was held over the body of Bob Prewitt. The jury returned a verdict from the evidence that Bob Prewitt came to his death from the effect of a gun-shot wound inflicted by ——, living in the town of Canton. Ben Fullbright is still alive, but is in a very critical condition. He says he knows who shot him. The sheriff is anxious to ferret out and bring to justice the guilty parties, but he can get no substantial support. A majority of the citizens, it is claimed, and some of the officials, are inclined to the opinion that the slayers are entitled to considerable sympathy. One leading citizen said he "would give a chromo to the person doing the shooting if he only knew who he was." Another said "he would give $25 to shake the hand of the person doing the shooting." The county attorney says he is afraid to go forward in the matter, as some one might slip up to his window some night and "plug him." So it is easy to imagine how powerless the law is in the matter under existing circumstances.

A negro church house was burned in the south portion of this county a few days since.

Commissioners court has been in session this week.

An election has been ordered in this county, to take place on the 8th of September, to determine whether or not the people want local option.

ITEMS FROM THE SOUTH.
A large and apparently inexhaustible bed of bituminous coal has been discovered within three miles of the city limits of Lampasas, Tex. Samples taken from the vein show a fine quality of coal, equal if not superior to the Indian Territory article.

Jake Evans, a negro, brutally assaulted a white woman at Auburn, Ala. He was arrested, but a mob overpowered the officers and hanged Evans to a tree.

The Secretary of the Treasury has been informed that Aufdemort, the defaulting officer at the Sub-Treasury in New Orleans, has fled to Mexico, where he is interested in some mines.

Attorney Ganeral Garland decides that the Interior Department has no power, under the law, to authorize the Indians to lease their lands for grazing purposes.

At a ball near Rogersville, Tenn., Miss Martha Brown, a beautiful girl, was shot and instantly killed by the explosion of a revolver which dropped from her partner's pocket while they were dancing.

James Hall, an aged farmer living near Savannah, Ga., caught his foot in a fence he was climbing, and hung head downward for three days before he was rescued. He will die.

The Superintendent of Public Instruction in Kansas, has unearthed a batch of school land frauds. He found parties hired at $2 a day to make purchases of the lands and then transfer their titles to their employers.

While under the influence of liquor, Henry Van Derfeight leaped from the suspension bridge across the Cumberland River at Nashville, Tenn., to the water below, a distance of 110 feet. He turned several times in the air and struck the water with terrific force. He will probably recover.
A BILL has been introduced in the Georgia Legislature making it unlawful for a member of the General assembly, or a judicial officer to use a free pass on a railroad.
CATERPILLARS have appeared in the cotton fields of several counties of South Carolina, and boll worms in one or two. Unless their ravages are great, the crop will be the largest for years.
jake-evans-auburn-1885-08.A3:
ITEMS FROM THE SOUTH.
DR. SWEARENGER, State Health Officer of Texas, has gone to El Paso to establish a quarantine there against yellow fever infected points in Mexico.

REV. J. R. SPECK, a prominent Methodist clergyman of Canton, Ga., attempted suicide by cutting his throat from ear to ear with a pocketknife. The wounds are not believed to be deep enough to produce death.

FOUR children of Susan Ashley, colored, living at Graham, Ga., who were left in the house alone, were burned to death.

THE drivers on the street car lines at Memphis, Tenn., have quit work on a strike against a reduction from 12¢ to 10 cents per hour.

THE Secretary of the Treasury has been informed that Aufdemort, the defaulting officer at the Sub-Treasury in New Orleans, has fled to Mexico, where he is interested in some mines.

AT Sedalia, Mo., Henry Toggenberger a young man from Bluffton, Ohio, was found dead in his bep with three ghastly wounds in his head, done with a hatchet. The perpetrator of the crime is not known, but he is supposed to be a man with whom Toggerberger had 'trouble about a woman.

WILLIAM HAMILTON and Variman Hamilton, two full-blood Chickasaw Indians, were convicted at Fort Smith, Ark., in the United States District Court, for the murder of A. Colbert in April, 1884. The murder occurred in the Chickasaw Nation, and was a cold-blooded affair. The jury were only out about twenty minutes.

JAKE EVANS, a negro, brutally assaulted a white woman at Auburn, Ala. He was arrested, but a mob overpowered the officers and hanged Evans to a tree.

Gov. HUBBARD, of Texas, is to supercede Gen. Bingham as United States Minister to Japan, and the latter will probably return to Congress from Ohio.

R. M. BUEHLER, a traveling man from St. Louis, committed suicide at the Windsor Hotel, in Atchison, Kan., by shooting himself through the brain. He leaves a wife and child in St. Louis.

The steamer Blue Wing, from the Kentucky River, reports that an old man named Willis Roch, having money on his person, was attacked by four unknown men near Frankfort, Ky. A young son of Roch came to his father's assistance, and with a pistol shot and killed two of the men, fatally wounding the third, and the fourth made his escape. The boat's crew gleaned this meager information from the inhabitants along the river.
